claim: Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP) is a disease of progressive heterotopic ossification caused by ACVR1R206H (Activin receptor type-1 receptor) mutation.
source: Here, we use fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP), a disease of progressive HO caused by ACVR1R206H (Activin receptor type-1 receptor) mutation, to elucidate how ACVR1 affects skeletal muscle repair.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about FOP.

claim: Primary FOP human muscle stem cells isolated from cadaveric skeletal muscle demonstrated increased extracellular matrix (ECM) marker expression.
source: Rare and unique primary FOP human muscle stem cells (Hu-MuSCs) isolated from cadaveric skeletal muscle demonstrated increased extracellular matric (ECM) marker expression, showed skeletal muscle-specific impaired engraftment and regeneration ability.
evidence: This finding is reported in the abstract as a result from the study.

claim: Primary FOP human muscle stem cells showed skeletal muscle-specific impaired engraftment and regeneration ability.
source: Rare and unique primary FOP human muscle stem cells (Hu-MuSCs) isolated from cadaveric skeletal muscle demonstrated increased extracellular matric (ECM) marker expression, showed skeletal muscle-specific impaired engraftment and regeneration ability.
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding reported in the abstract.

claim: Human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived muscle stem/progenitor cells (iMPCs) from FOP revealed unusually increased ECM and osteogenic marker expression compared to control iMPCs.
source: Human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived muscle stem/progenitor cells (iMPCs) single-cell transcriptome analyses from FOP also revealed unusually increased ECM and osteogenic marker expression compared to control iMPCs.
evidence: This is a direct finding from single-cell transcriptome analysis reported in the abstract.

claim: ACVR1 is a key regulator of human muscle stem cell function and skeletal muscle repair.
source: These results show that iMPCs can recapitulate many aspects of Hu-MuSCs for detailed in vitro study; that ACVR1 is a key regulator of Hu-MuSC function and skeletal muscle repair; and that ACVR1 activation in iMPCs or Hu-MuSCs may contribute to HO by changing the local tissue environment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented in the study.

claim: ACVR1 activation in iMPCs or Hu-MuSCs may contribute to heterotopic ossification by changing the local tissue environment.
source: These results show that iMPCs can recapitulate many aspects of Hu-MuSCs for detailed in vitro study; that ACVR1 is a key regulator of Hu-MuSC function and skeletal muscle repair; and that ACVR1 activation in iMPCs or Hu-MuSCs may contribute to HO by changing the local tissue environment.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Heterotopic ossification can form after trauma, burns, spinal cord injuries, and surgical procedures such as hip arthroplasty.
source: Although HO is a relatively uncommon complication, it can form after trauma, burns, spinal cord injuries, and surgical procedures such as hip arthroplasty (Agarwal et al., 2016; Matsuo et al., 2019; Meyers et al., 2019; Sullivan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Heterotopic ossification has been reported in patients with severe COVID-19.
source: Recently, HO has been reported in patients with severe COVID-19, suggesting a critical role for inflammation and muscle damage (Aziz et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a 2021 publication.

claim: The majority of FOP patients have the classical ACVR1R206H (c.617> A) mutation.
source: FOP is a congenital disease of abnormal skeletal muscle regeneration and severe HO, in which the majority of patients have the classical ACVR1R206H (c.617> A) mutation (Shore Eileen et al., 2006) that causes hyperactivation of the BMP-SMAD signaling (Billings et al., 2008) and aberrant responses to Activin A (Hatsell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shore et al., 2006.

claim: The ACVR1R206H mutation causes hyperactivation of the BMP-SMAD signaling.
source: FOP is a congenital disease of abnormal skeletal muscle regeneration and severe HO, in which the majority of patients have the classical ACVR1R206H (c.617> A) mutation (Shore Eileen et al., 2006) that causes hyperactivation of the BMP-SMAD signaling (Billings et al., 2008) and aberrant responses to Activin A (Hatsell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Billings et al., 2008.

claim: The ACVR1R206H mutation causes aberrant responses to Activin A.
source: FOP is a congenital disease of abnormal skeletal muscle regeneration and severe HO, in which the majority of patients have the classical ACVR1R206H (c.617> A) mutation (Shore Eileen et al., 2006) that causes hyperactivation of the BMP-SMAD signaling (Billings et al., 2008) and aberrant responses to Activin A (Hatsell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hatsell et al., 2015.

claim: Multiple cell types including endothelial cells, mesenchymal progenitors, pericytes, mast cells, macrophages, and FAPs can contribute to heterotopic ossification in FOP.
source: While previous studies suggested that multiple cell types including endothelial cells (Barruet et al., 2016; Medici et al., 2010), mesenchymal progenitors (Culbert et al., 2014; Dey et al., 2016), pericytes (Cai et al., 2015), and more recently mast cells (Brennan et al., 2018; Convente et al., 2018), macrophages (Barruet et al., 2018; Matsuo et al., 2021), and FAPs (Lees-Shepard et al., 2018) can indirectly or directly contribute to HO in FOP, how the ACVR1R206H mutation impairs human muscle repair and muscle stem cell function has yet to be determined.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs) were originally identified by their ability to induce bone formation when injected into muscle.
source: Disrupted signaling of bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs), originally identified by their ability to induce bone formation when injected into muscle (Urist, 1965), changes muscle homeostasis (Ono et al., 2011) by controlling the proliferation and differentiation of satellite cells (SCs) (Ono et al., 2011; Stantzou et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Urist, 1965.

claim: Disrupted BMP signaling changes muscle homeostasis by controlling the proliferation and differentiation of satellite cells.
source: Disrupted signaling of bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs), originally identified by their ability to induce bone formation when injected into muscle (Urist, 1965), changes muscle homeostasis (Ono et al., 2011) by controlling the proliferation and differentiation of satellite cells (SCs) (Ono et al., 2011; Stantzou et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ono et al., 2011 and Stantzou et al., 2017.

claim: Satellite cells marked by PAX7 are a prerequisite for skeletal muscle regeneration.
source: SCs marked by PAX7 (Paired Box 7) (Seale et al., 2000), are a prerequisite for skeletal muscle regeneration (Mauro, 1961) and are thought to be the main human muscle stem cells (Hu-MuSCs) of postnatal skeletal muscle.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Seale et al., 2000 and Mauro, 1961.

claim: Upon injury, activated satellite cells give rise to myoblasts, which form new myofibers or fuse to existing muscle fibers to repair muscle damage.
source: Upon injury, activated SCs give rise to myoblasts, which form new myofibers or fuse to existing muscle fibers to repair muscle damage (Kuang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kuang et al., 2007.

claim: The BMP pathway is critical for maintaining PAX7 expression in primary muscle stem cells and for preventing commitment to myogenic differentiation.
source: The BMP pathway is critical for maintaining PAX7 expression in primary MuSCs and for preventing commitment to myogenic differentiation (Friedrichs et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Friedrichs et al., 2011.

claim: Abrogation of BMP signaling in satellite cells slowed myofiber growth.
source: Abrogation of BMP signaling in SCs slowed myofiber growth (Stantzou et al., 2017), and increased BMP4 levels in Duchenne's muscular dystrophy (DMD) can exacerbate the disease (Shi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stantzou et al., 2017.

claim: Increased BMP4 levels in Duchenne's muscular dystrophy can exacerbate the disease.
source: Abrogation of BMP signaling in SCs slowed myofiber growth (Stantzou et al., 2017), and increased BMP4 levels in Duchenne's muscular dystrophy (DMD) can exacerbate the disease (Shi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shi et al., 2013.

claim: BMP signaling is a key pathway that can be manipulated to make human muscle stem cell-like cells from hiPSCs.
source: Interestingly, BMP signaling is a key pathway that can be manipulated to make Hu-MuSCs-like cells from hiPSCs (iMPCs) (Chal et al., 2016; Chal et al., 2018; Xi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chal et al., 2016, 2018 and Xi et al., 2017.

claim: Recent protocols to create human muscle stem cell-like cells from hiPSCs could generate skeletal myogenic lineage cells, but with limited muscle regenerative capacity.
source: Recent protocols to create Hu-MuSCs-like cells from hiPSCs (Takahashi et al., 2007) could generate skeletal myogenic lineage cells, but with limited muscle regenerative capacity (Borchin et al., 2013; Magli et al., 2017; Shelton et al., 2014; van der Wal et al., 2018; Xi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Transgene-induced PAX7 or PAX3 expression in hiPSCs can increase engraftment of PAX7+ cells and contribution to the satellite cell pool.
source: Transgene-induced PAX7 or PAX3 expression in hiPSCs can increase engraftment of PAX7+ cells and contribution to the SC pool (Al Tanoury et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2018); however, these engineered cells may not reflect physiology due to the genetic manipulation of these master transcription factors.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Al Tanoury et al., 2020 and Wu et al., 2018.

claim: FOP muscle tissue near a heterotopic ossification lesion showed increased ECM proteoglycan components in the interstitial space of the muscle fibers.
source: FOP muscle tissue near a HO lesion showed increased ECM proteoglycan components (alcian blue staining) in the interstitial space of the muscle fibers near the HO lesion (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from histological staining shown in Figure 1A.

claim: PAX7 staining confirmed the presence of satellite cells in human FOP biceps.
source: PAX7 staining confirmed the presence of SCs in human FOP biceps (Figure 1B, middle and right).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A small subregion of FOP biceps showed Collagen Type 1 expression with embedded satellite cells suggesting possible early heterotopic ossification formation.
source: Interestingly, a small subregion showed Collagen Type 1 expression with embedded satellite cells (Figure 1B, right) suggesting possible early HO formation despite absence of gross HO.
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence staining with an inference about early HO formation.

claim: FOP human muscle stem cells showed lower PAX7 expression compared to control human muscle stem cells.
source: FOP Hu-MuSCs showed lower PAX7 expression compared to control Hu-MuSCs.
evidence: This is a direct finding from gene expression analysis.

claim: COL1A1 and ID3 were increased in affected FOP muscle (biceps).
source: COL1A1 and ID3 were increased in affected FOP muscle (biceps) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct finding from gene expression analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ID1 was increased in both the FOP diaphragm and biceps compared to control muscles.
source: However, ID1 was increased in both the FOP diaphragm and biceps compared to control muscles (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct finding from gene expression analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The number of human DYSTROPHIN-positive fibers was significantly lower with FOP human muscle stem cells versus control human muscle stem cells at 5 weeks after transplantation.
source: However, the number of human DYSTROPHIN-positive fibers was significantly lower with FOP Hu-MuSCs vs. control Hu-MuSCs (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a direct finding from quantification of immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The number of human DYSTROPHIN fibers was significantly decreased when FOP biceps human muscle stem cells were transplanted compared to control human muscle stem cells at 10 weeks after re-injury.
source: Ten weeks after re-injury with bupivacaine at week 5 (Figure 1D), the number of human DYSTROPHIN fibers was significantly decreased when FOP biceps Hu-MuSCs were transplanted compared to control Hu-MuSCs, but not when FOP diaphragm Hu-MuSCs were transplanted (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This is a direct finding from quantification of immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: The number of human DYSTROPHIN fibers was not significantly decreased when FOP diaphragm human muscle stem cells were transplanted compared to control human muscle stem cells at 10 weeks after re-injury.
source: Ten weeks after re-injury with bupivacaine at week 5 (Figure 1D), the number of human DYSTROPHIN fibers was significantly decreased when FOP biceps Hu-MuSCs were transplanted compared to control Hu-MuSCs, but not when FOP diaphragm Hu-MuSCs were transplanted (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This is a direct finding from quantification of immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: No radiologic evidence of heterotopic ossification was found in any mice after transplantation of human muscle stem cells.
source: No radiologic evidence of HO was found in any mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from X-ray imaging shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The source of FOP human muscle stem cells (biceps or diaphragm) may impact muscle stem cell engraftment efficiency.
source: In addition, the results suggest that the source of FOP Hu-MuSCs (biceps or diaphragm) may impact MuSC engraftment efficiency.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential engraftment results between biceps and diaphragm-derived cells.

claim: Control hiPSCs yielded PAX7, MYOGENIN-expressing cells.
source: The control hiPSCs yielded PAX7, MYOGENIN-expressing cells (Figure 2B and C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), expressed DYSTROPHIN (Figure 2B), and formed contractile myotubes (Figure 2C; Video 1 and Video 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Control hiPSCs expressed DYSTROPHIN.
source: The control hiPSCs yielded PAX7, MYOGENIN-expressing cells (Figure 2B and C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), expressed DYSTROPHIN (Figure 2B), and formed contractile myotubes (Figure 2C; Video 1 and Video 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Control hiPSCs formed contractile myotubes.
source: The control hiPSCs yielded PAX7, MYOGENIN-expressing cells (Figure 2B and C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), expressed DYSTROPHIN (Figure 2B), and formed contractile myotubes (Figure 2C; Video 1 and Video 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from imaging shown in Figure 2C and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: All three FOP iPSC lines formed contractile myotubes with cells expressing PAX7, MYOGENIN, and DYSTROPHIN.
source: All three FOP iPSC lines formed contractile myotubes with cells expressing PAX7, MYOGENIN, and DYSTROPHIN (Figure 2B and C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunofluorescence staining and imaging shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Adding a SMAD inhibitor of the BMP pathway (LDN193189) into the differentiation protocol improved the differentiation of the control hiPSC lines.
source: Adding a SMAD inhibitor of the BMP pathway (LDN193189) into the differentiation protocol (Figure 2E) improved the differentiation of the control hiPSC lines.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the differentiation experiments.

claim: LDN193189 improved differentiation of the FOP F3-2 line, which had shown lower PAX7 and MYOGENIN expression.
source: LDN also improved differentiation of the FOP F3-2 (Figure 2F) line, which had shown lower PAX7 and MYOGENIN expression (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the differentiation experiments shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Individual hiPSC lines are heterogeneous in differentiation to skeletal muscle lineages.
source: These findings show that individual hiPSC lines are heterogeneous in differentiation to skeletal muscle lineages, similar to other protocols (Volpato and Webber, 2020), that FOP hiPSCs can form skeletal muscle cells and Hu-MuSC-like cells expressing PAX7 despite upregulation of the BMP pathway by ACVR1R206H, and that chemical blockade of the BMP pathway can improve the formation of Hu-MuSC-like cells from the FOP iPSC line that showed the lowest efficiency.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results and supported by a citation to Volpato and Webber, 2020.

claim: FOP hiPSCs can form skeletal muscle cells and human muscle stem cell-like cells expressing PAX7 despite upregulation of the BMP pathway by ACVR1R206H.
source: These findings show that individual hiPSC lines are heterogeneous in differentiation to skeletal muscle lineages, similar to other protocols (Volpato and Webber, 2020), that FOP hiPSCs can form skeletal muscle cells and Hu-MuSC-like cells expressing PAX7 despite upregulation of the BMP pathway by ACVR1R206H, and that chemical blockade of the BMP pathway can improve the formation of Hu-MuSC-like cells from the FOP iPSC line that showed the lowest efficiency.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Chemical blockade of the BMP pathway can improve the formation of human muscle stem cell-like cells from the FOP iPSC line that showed the lowest efficiency.
source: These findings show that individual hiPSC lines are heterogeneous in differentiation to skeletal muscle lineages, similar to other protocols (Volpato and Webber, 2020), that FOP hiPSCs can form skeletal muscle cells and Hu-MuSC-like cells expressing PAX7 despite upregulation of the BMP pathway by ACVR1R206H, and that chemical blockade of the BMP pathway can improve the formation of Hu-MuSC-like cells from the FOP iPSC line that showed the lowest efficiency.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results with LDN193189.

claim: FACS analysis identified intermediate CD56 cells expressing high PAX7 and low MYOGENIN.
source: FACS analysis identified intermediate CD56 cells expressing high PAX7 and low MYOGENIN (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D), consistent with Hu-MuSC expression profiles.
evidence: This is a direct observation from FACS analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: All HNK1-CD45-CD31- CXCR4+CD29+CD56dim cells formed myotubes expressing MHC when cultured in terminal differentiation media.
source: All HNK1-CD45-CD31- CXCR4+CD29+CD56dim cells formed myotubes expressing MHC (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) when cultured in terminal differentiation media demonstrating isolation of functional iMPCs with satellite cell-like characteristics from the cultures.
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: iMPCs derived from control or FOP hiPSCs can engraft and promote muscle regeneration in NSG mice.
source: New fibers expressing human DYSTROPHIN and PAX7 cells were found after 5 weeks, showing that iMPCs could engraft and promote muscle regeneration (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The number of human fibers and human PAX7+ cells remained low with iMPCs compared to primary human muscle stem cells.
source: However, the number of human fibers and human PAX7+ cells remained low (Figure 3D) compared to primary Hu-MuSCs.
evidence: This is a direct observation from quantification shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 2000 primary non-FOP human muscle stem cells resulted in an average of 155 human fibers based on prior assessments using the same assay.
source: By comparison, 2000 primary non-FOP Hu-MuSCs resulted in an average of 155 human fibers based on prior assessments using the same assay (Garcia Steven et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior published results cited from Garcia et al., 2018.

claim: No significant differences between control and FOP iMPCs were identified in engraftment assays.
source: No significant differences between control and FOP iMPCs were identified, though some individual FOP samples showed higher engraftment (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a direct finding from the quantification shown in Figure 3D.

claim: iMPCs have engraftment potential into a muscle injury site in mice.
source: These results showed that iMPCs have engraftment potential into a muscle injury site in mice, but engraftment efficiency may be lower than primary Hu-MuSCs or be the result of differences in experimental conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the transplantation experiments.

claim: ACVR1R206H did not significantly impact muscle fiber regeneration in the iMPC transplantation assay.
source: Also, ACVR1R206H did not significantly impact muscle fiber regeneration in this assay.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of significant differences between control and FOP iMPCs.

claim: Both control and FOP iMPC samples had clusters expressing myogenic genes (PAX7 and MYOD), mesenchymal genes (PDGFRA), and neuronal genes (SOX2).
source: Both control (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and FOP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) samples had clusters expressing myogenic genes (PAX7 and MYOD); mesenchymal genes (PDGFRA); and neuronal genes (SOX2) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a direct finding from single-cell RNA sequencing analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cells expressing muscle markers (PAX7, MYF5, MYOD, and MYOG) were found in clusters 0–2.
source: Cells expressing muscle markers (PAX7, MYF5, MYOD, and MYOG [MYOGENIN]) were found in clusters 0–2 (Figure 4B–C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a direct finding from single-cell RNA sequencing analysis shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Mesenchymal genes (PDGFRA, ASPN, and COL1A1) were expressed in cluster 3.
source: Mesenchymal genes (PDGFRA, ASPN, and COL1A1) were expressed in cluster 3.
evidence: This is a direct finding from single-cell RNA sequencing analysis.

claim: The frequency of muscle cells (clusters 0–2) was higher in FOP (14%, 2.5%, and 1.7%) compared to controls (4.2%, 0.5%, and 0.5%).
source: The frequency of muscle cells (clusters 0–2) was higher in FOP (14%, 2.5%, and 1.7%) compared to controls (4.2%, 0.5%, and 0.5%) (Figure 4F) suggesting that FOP hiPSCs may be more efficient at making muscle progenitor cells.
evidence: This is a direct finding from single-cell RNA sequencing analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: FOP hiPSCs may be more efficient at making muscle progenitor cells.
source: The frequency of muscle cells (clusters 0–2) was higher in FOP (14%, 2.5%, and 1.7%) compared to controls (4.2%, 0.5%, and 0.5%) (Figure 4F) suggesting that FOP hiPSCs may be more efficient at making muscle progenitor cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the higher frequency of muscle cells in FOP cultures.

claim: FACS-purified iMPC cultures contain muscle stem/progenitor cells, but other cell types such as mesenchymal, neuronal progenitor cells, and myoblasts persist in the culture.
source: Thus, FACS-purified iMPC cultures contain muscle stem/progenitor cells, but other cell types such as mesenchymal, neuronal progenitor cells, and myoblasts persist in the culture.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the single-cell RNA sequencing analysis showing multiple cell types.

claim: The frequency of iMPCs appears to be higher in FOP vs. control cell cultures.
source: Furthermore, the frequency of iMPCs appears to be higher in FOP vs. control cell cultures.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the single-cell RNA sequencing analysis.

claim: Clusters 0–3 expressed higher levels of PAX7 and MYF5 (markers of more quiescent muscle stem cells) while cluster four expressed higher levels of MYOD, MYOG, SOX8, and MEF2C (markers of differentiated muscle stem cells/myoblasts/myocytes).
source: Clusters 0–3 expressed higher levels of PAX7 and MYF5 (markers of more quiescent MuSCs) while cluster four expressed higher levels of MYOD (or MYOD1), MYOG, SOX8, and MEF2C (markers of differentiated MuSCs/myoblasts/myocytes).
evidence: This is a direct finding from sub-clustering analysis of myogenic cells.

claim: Muscle stem-like cells expressing APOE, KRT17, and CAV1 defined cluster 0.
source: Muscle stem-like cells expressing APOE, KRT17, and CAV1 defined cluster 0.
evidence: This is a direct finding from sub-clustering analysis of myogenic cells.

claim: Quiescence markers (SPRY1, HEY1, HES1) were highly expressed in cluster 0.
source: Quiescence markers (SPRY1, HEY1, HES1) were also highly expressed in this cluster.
evidence: This is a direct finding from sub-clustering analysis of myogenic cells.

claim: CDH15, a niche regulator of satellite cell quiescence, was enriched in cluster 1.
source: CDH15, a niche regulator of SCs quiescence (Goel et al., 2017) was enriched in cluster 1.
evidence: This is a direct finding from sub-clustering analysis with a citation to Goel et al., 2017.

claim: Cluster 3 had a higher proportion of cells in G2M and S phase.
source: Cluster 3 had a higher proportion of cells in G2M and S phase (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B (left)).
evidence: This is a direct finding from cell cycle analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The cell cycle distribution was similar in control and FOP.
source: The cell cycle distribution was similar in control and FOP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B (right)).
evidence: This is a direct finding from cell cycle analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The proportion of cells in clusters 0 and 3 was higher in FOP (31.4% and 23.4%) compared to control (20% and 5.5%).
source: The proportion of cells in clusters 0 and 3 was higher in FOP (31.4% and 23.4%) compared to control (20% and 5.5%), while the proportion of cells in cluster two was increased in control (51.8% vs 21.9%) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a direct finding from sub-clustering analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The proportion of cells in cluster two was increased in control (51.8%) compared to FOP (21.9%).
source: The proportion of cells in clusters 0 and 3 was higher in FOP (31.4% and 23.4%) compared to control (20% and 5.5%), while the proportion of cells in cluster two was increased in control (51.8% vs 21.9%) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a direct finding from sub-clustering analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: PAX7 and MYF5 were upregulated in branch A but downregulated in the tip of branches B and C.
source: PAX7 and MYF5 were upregulated in branch A but downregulated in the tip of branches B and C (Figure 5C and E) confirming the correct cell ordering.
evidence: This is a direct finding from pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5C and E.

claim: MYOD and MYOG showed higher expression patterns early in branch B and late in branch C.
source: MYOD and MYOG showed higher expression patterns early in branch B and late in branch C (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is a direct finding from pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: hiPSC differentiation cultures contain subpopulations of iMPCs showing the expected spectrum of quiescence, activation, and differentiation.
source: Thus, hiPSC differentiation cultures contain subpopulations of iMPCs showing the expected spectrum of quiescence, activation, and differentiation with FOP cultures having a higher proportion of cells in the stem cell/progenitor and proliferating phases and fewer mature myoblasts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pseudotime trajectory analysis.

claim: FOP cultures have a higher proportion of cells in the stem cell/progenitor and proliferating phases and fewer mature myoblasts.
source: Thus, hiPSC differentiation cultures contain subpopulations of iMPCs showing the expected spectrum of quiescence, activation, and differentiation with FOP cultures having a higher proportion of cells in the stem cell/progenitor and proliferating phases and fewer mature myoblasts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pseudotime trajectory analysis.

claim: PAX7 was significantly increased in control vs. FOP cells in cluster three only.
source: While PAX7 was significantly increased in control vs. FOP cells in cluster three only, MYF5 was significantly increased in FOP cells from cluster 1 compared to control cells (Figure 5G, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct finding from differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: MYF5 was significantly increased in FOP cells from cluster 1 compared to control cells.
source: While PAX7 was significantly increased in control vs. FOP cells in cluster three only, MYF5 was significantly increased in FOP cells from cluster 1 compared to control cells (Figure 5G, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct finding from differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: SPRY1, a known regulator of quiescence which decreases with age, was significantly downregulated in FOP cells in all the clusters.
source: Interestingly, SPRY1, a known regulator of quiescence (Shea et al., 2010) which decreases with age (Bigot et al., 2015), was significantly downregulated in FOP cells in all the clusters, while DLK1, which act as a muscle regeneration inhibitor (Andersen et al., 2013) was significantly increased in FOP cells (Figure 5G and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct finding from differential expression analysis with citations to Shea et al., 2010 and Bigot et al., 2015.

claim: DLK1, which acts as a muscle regeneration inhibitor, was significantly increased in FOP cells.
source: Interestingly, SPRY1, a known regulator of quiescence (Shea et al., 2010) which decreases with age (Bigot et al., 2015), was significantly downregulated in FOP cells in all the clusters, while DLK1, which act as a muscle regeneration inhibitor (Andersen et al., 2013) was significantly increased in FOP cells (Figure 5G and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct finding from differential expression analysis with a citation to Andersen et al., 2013.

claim: ITM2A, COL1A1, DCN, CD151, SPARC, and TIMP1 were significantly increased in FOP cells.
source: ITM2A, COL1A1, DCN, CD151, SPARC, and TIMP1 were significantly increased in FOP cells (Figure 5H, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct finding from differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: ECM proteoglycans known to be involved in inflammation, including BGN and LUM, were increased in FOP cells.
source: ECM proteoglycans known to be involved in inflammation, including BGN (Nastase et al., 2012) and LUM (Nikitovic et al., 2014), TAGLN which regulates osteogenic differentiation (Elsafadi et al., 2016), and IGBP5 which is increased in aged satellite cells (Soriano-Arroquia et al., 2016), were also increased in FOP cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a direct finding from differential expression analysis with citations to Nastase et al., 2012 and Nikitovic et al., 2014.

claim: TAGLN which regulates osteogenic differentiation was increased in FOP cells.
source: ECM proteoglycans known to be involved in inflammation, including BGN (Nastase et al., 2012) and LUM (Nikitovic et al., 2014), TAGLN which regulates osteogenic differentiation (Elsafadi et al., 2016), and IGBP5 which is increased in aged satellite cells (Soriano-Arroquia et al., 2016), were also increased in FOP cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a direct finding from differential expression analysis with a citation to Elsafadi et al., 2016.

claim: IGBP5 which is increased in aged satellite cells was increased in FOP cells.
source: ECM proteoglycans known to be involved in inflammation, including BGN (Nastase et al., 2012) and LUM (Nikitovic et al., 2014), TAGLN which regulates osteogenic differentiation (Elsafadi et al., 2016), and IGBP5 which is increased in aged satellite cells (Soriano-Arroquia et al., 2016), were also increased in FOP cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a direct finding from differential expression analysis with a citation to Soriano-Arroquia et al., 2016.

claim: A higher number of cells expressed SOX9 in FOP than control cells.
source: However, a higher number of cells expressed SOX9 in FOP than control cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F-G).
evidence: This is a direct finding from differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F-G.

claim: ID1 was significantly higher in clusters 0, 1, 3, and 4 in control cells.
source: ID1 was significantly higher in clusters 0 (MuSCs 1), 1 (MPCs), 3 (Cycling MuSCs), and 4 (Myoblasts) in control cells, while ID3 was significantly higher in FOP cells clusters 1 (MPCs) and 2 (MuSC 2).
evidence: This is a direct finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: ID3 was significantly higher in FOP cells clusters 1 and 2.
source: ID1 was significantly higher in clusters 0 (MuSCs 1), 1 (MPCs), 3 (Cycling MuSCs), and 4 (Myoblasts) in control cells, while ID3 was significantly higher in FOP cells clusters 1 (MPCs) and 2 (MuSC 2).
evidence: This is a direct finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: The BMP/TGFβ pathway downstream target gene SMAD5 was significantly higher in cluster 2 of control cells.
source: In addition, the BMP/TGFβ pathway downstream target gene SMAD5 was significantly higher in cluster 2 (MuSCs 2) of control cells.
evidence: This is a direct finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: The p38 pathway components JUN, JUNB, and FOS were significantly increased in FOP cells.
source: The p38 pathway components JUN (clusters 1, 3), JUNB (clusters 0–2), and FOS (clusters 1, 3) were significantly increased in FOP cells.
evidence: This is a direct finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: BMPR2 and ACVR2B expression were significantly higher in control cells.
source: Within the known ACVR1 co-receptors, BMPR2 (clusters 3, 4) and ACVR2B (clusters 0, 2, 3) expression were significantly higher in control cells while ACVR2A expression was significantly higher in FOP cells (clusters 1, 4).
evidence: This is a direct finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: ACVR2A expression was significantly higher in FOP cells.
source: Within the known ACVR1 co-receptors, BMPR2 (clusters 3, 4) and ACVR2B (clusters 0, 2, 3) expression were significantly higher in control cells while ACVR2A expression was significantly higher in FOP cells (clusters 1, 4).
evidence: This is a direct finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: FOP iMPCs may have a chondrogenic/osteogenic signature, increased ID3 expression, and higher p38 pathway activity and higher levels of the ACVR2A co-receptor at different stages of myogenic differentiation.
source: Similar to the primary FOP Hu-MuSCs (Figure 1), these results suggest that FOP iMPCs may have a chondrogenic/osteogenic signature, increased ID3 expression, and also showed higher p38 pathway activity and higher levels of the ACVR2A co-receptor at different stages of myogenic differentiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential expression analysis.

claim: PAX7 and MYF5 gene expression levels were higher in primary human muscle stem cells than in iMPCs.
source: Although iMPCs expressed PAX7 and MYF5, the gene expression levels were higher in primary Hu-MuSCs.
evidence: This is a direct finding from comparing iMPCs to primary Hu-MuSCs.

claim: MYOD was higher in iMPCs than in primary human muscle stem cells.
source: In contrast, MYOD was higher in iMPCs (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct finding from comparing iMPCs to primary Hu-MuSCs shown in Figure 6C.

claim: iMPCs ordered away from primary human muscle stem cells and primary myocytes in pseudotime trajectory analysis.
source: iMPCs ordered away from primary Hu-MuSCs (PAX7+) and primary myocytes (MYL1+) (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: This is a direct finding from pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 6E-G.

claim: Branch B consisted of iMPCs and subset of primary human muscle stem cells, and expressed significantly higher levels of genes associated with mesenchymal, fibrogenic, chondrogenic, osteogenic lineages and extracellular matrix.
source: Branch A was mainly constituted of primary Hu-MuSCs while branch B consisted of iMPCs and subset of primary Hu-MuSCs, expressed significantly higher levels of genes associated with mesenchymal, fibrogenic, chondrogenic, osteogenic lineages and extracellular matrix (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: This is a direct finding from branch expression analysis shown in Figure 6G and H.

claim: iMPCs retained strong bi-potency compared to primary human muscle stem cells.
source: Thus, iMPCs retained strong bi-potency compared to primary Hu-MuSCs, suggesting that iMPCs may not be as committed to the muscle lineage as primary adult muscle stem cells (Xi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the branch expression analysis with a citation to Xi et al., 2020.

claim: iMPCs may not be as committed to the muscle lineage as primary adult muscle stem cells.

claim: The iMPC system revealed that activation of the BMP pathway by the FOP ACVR1R206H mutation induced changes that could contribute to abnormal muscle healing.
source: This iMPC system revealed that activation of the BMP pathway by the FOP ACVR1R206H mutation induced changes that could contribute to abnormal muscle healing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The classical SMAD pathways were active in FOP cells.
source: As expected, the classical SMAD pathways were active in FOP cells; however, it was unexpected to find that the p38 pathway via JUN/FOS was more active in the FOP iMPCs, considering that FOP cultures had a higher proportion of cells in the stem cell/progenitor and proliferating phases.
evidence: This is a direct finding from the differential expression analysis.

claim: The p38 pathway via JUN/FOS was more active in the FOP iMPCs.
source: As expected, the classical SMAD pathways were active in FOP cells; however, it was unexpected to find that the p38 pathway via JUN/FOS was more active in the FOP iMPCs, considering that FOP cultures had a higher proportion of cells in the stem cell/progenitor and proliferating phases.
evidence: This is a direct finding from the differential expression analysis.

claim: Abnormal SMAD activity or misinterpretation of the Activin A ligand occur with the ACVR1R206H mutation.
source: While increased SMAD activity (Billings et al., 2008) or misinterpretation of the Activin A ligand (Hatsell et al., 2015) occur with the ACVR1R206H mutation, abnormal p38 signaling may be critical in some cell types like macrophages (Barruet et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Billings et al., 2008 and Hatsell et al., 2015.

claim: Abnormal p38 signaling may be critical in some cell types like macrophages.
source: While increased SMAD activity (Billings et al., 2008) or misinterpretation of the Activin A ligand (Hatsell et al., 2015) occur with the ACVR1R206H mutation, abnormal p38 signaling may be critical in some cell types like macrophages (Barruet et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Barruet et al., 2018.

claim: p38 is a major regulator of human muscle stem cell function.
source: Since p38 is a major regulator of Hu-MuSC function (Segalés et al., 2016) and has been associated with inflammation and ECM accumulation in aged muscle (Cosgrove et al., 2014), further studies are needed to determine how this p38 signaling contributes to satellite cell subtype specification (Barruet et al., 2020) and affect healing in FOP.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Segalés et al., 2016.

claim: p38 has been associated with inflammation and ECM accumulation in aged muscle.
source: Since p38 is a major regulator of Hu-MuSC function (Segalés et al., 2016) and has been associated with inflammation and ECM accumulation in aged muscle (Cosgrove et al., 2014), further studies are needed to determine how this p38 signaling contributes to satellite cell subtype specification (Barruet et al., 2020) and affect healing in FOP.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cosgrove et al., 2014.

claim: iMPC and human muscle stem cell transplant studies showed no heterotopic ossification in the recipient mice.
source: Importantly, our iMPC and Hu-MuSC transplant studies showed no HO in the recipient mice, consistent with prior FOP genetic studies (Dey et al., 2016; Lees-Shepard et al., 2018) describing that other cell types may be directly responsible for bone formation.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the transplantation experiments.

claim: Aged muscle shows increased myofiber stiffness due to increased ECM deposition.
source: This has also been reported in aged muscle, which show increased myofiber stiffness due to increased ECM deposition (Hwang and Brack, 2018).

claim: Activated ACVR1 by the R206H mutation decreased (but did not abrogate) in vitro formation of mature myoblasts of FOP hiPSCs.
source: In addition, while our results suggest no major differences or possibly a slight increase in the ability to form skeletal muscle progenitors, activated ACVR1 by the R206H mutation decreased (but did not abrogate) in vitro formation of mature myoblasts of FOP hiPSCs and in vivo muscle repair after transplant of primary FOP Hu-MuSCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Activated ACVR1 by the R206H mutation decreased in vivo muscle repair after transplant of primary FOP human muscle stem cells.

claim: The clinical sparing of the diaphragm from heterotopic ossification in patients with FOP may result from a less impaired or unimpaired muscle repair process in diaphragm satellite cells.
